text:
No one cheers for you keeping the loan you already have.

Nobody posts about the refinance they didn’t do, the car they didn’t finance, the offset they didn’t touch.

The reason so few people end up with real equity is that the boring decisions never look impressive in the moment, only at the end.

The bank will tell you the most you can borrow.

Nobody tells you the most you can comfortably repay.

Those are different numbers. We quote the second one first, because approval and affordability are not the same thing, and living at the edge of what a lender will give you rarely buys a better life.

Everyone compares rates. Almost nobody compares structures.

A rate changes every few months. A structure decides what you can do for the next ten years.

If all you want is a sharper rate, call your bank. We’re here for how the loan is built.

Interest on your investment loan is usually deductible.

Interest on the home you live in isn’t.

So every spare dollar has a better home. It’s just not the one most people send it to. Worth a conversation with your accountant.

Redraw feels like savings. It isn’t.

It’s money you’ve already paid off your home loan. Pull it out for an investment and you’ve muddied what that loan was for.

A separate split for the investment keeps the story clean. Your accountant will thank you later.

Buying your first home? The loan is the easy bit.

The hard part is knowing whether the place is good value, what to offer, when to walk, and what the contract actually says.

You do the inspecting. We do the data, the digging and the negotiation, all the way to the keys.

The bank said no.

That’s one bank. One credit team, one policy, one way of reading your payslips.

It isn’t the answer. Half the files we end up settling were a no somewhere else first, because the income was real but the story was told badly.

Sign for thirty years. Pay it off in twenty-five anyway.

The longer term sets a lower minimum repayment, and the minimum is what every lender uses to work out what else you can borrow.

What’s on paper and what you actually do can be two different things.

The buyer’s agent says buy first.

The selling agent says sell first.

Both are good at their jobs. Both are also describing the order that pays them. Run the numbers with someone who gets paid the same either way, then let the agents do what they’re good at.

A bigger deposit feels safer. A buffer usually is.

If you qualify for a low-deposit scheme, we often prefer using it and keeping part of your savings back in an offset.

A slightly bigger loan with money behind you beats a smaller loan and an empty account.

Five boring money decisions that quietly build equity.

None of them will impress anyone at a barbecue.

All of them show up on your loan balance in five years.

Your pay lands in the offset, not a savings account.

Savings interest gets taxed. Offset interest saved doesn’t.

Same money, one of them is working harder for you.

Upsizing? Keep cash back for the first two or three years.

A slightly smaller deposit and a healthy offset beats tipping everything in.

The buffer is there while you get used to the bigger repayment.

Don’t ask how much buffer you have.

Ask how many months it buys.

A lump sum is just anxiety. A number of months is a plan with a review date.

Most people buy a car within six months of buying a home.

Plan it before the loan settles, not after it has eaten your budget.

The mortgage was never the thing that made the repayments tight.

What a broker actually does, in five lines.

Not the version on the website.

The version that explains why some clients stay for fifteen years.

You don’t pay us. The bank does, and every bank pays about the same.

So we don’t have a favourite.

The only thing that moves our recommendation is your file.

We ask every bank before we tell them who you are.

Then we apply once.

One application on your file, to the lender that already said yes in principle.

If your broker only talked about rate, you got a transaction, not advice.

Rates change every few months.

Structure is the thing that decides what you can do next.

Settlement isn’t the end. It’s where our job starts again.

Rate reviews, an equity check, a call when something in your life changes.

That’s the part nobody puts on the website either.

Buying an investment with your home’s equity?

The loan you get is easy. The structure you get is what matters.

Five lines we keep coming back to.

Keep the two properties in separate lanes.

The deposit comes from its own split against your home. Nothing is tied to anything else.

Separate security is what keeps you flexible later.

Equity sitting in an offset costs you nothing until you use it.

Set the facility up now, park it, and the repayment is effectively zero.

You move when the right property turns up, not when the bank is ready.

Investment debt stays interest-only. Your repayments go at the home loan.

One of those interest bills is usually deductible. One never is.

Your accountant should be in this conversation.

Transact through the offset. Never through redraw.

And set up today’s loan for the property after this one.

Restructuring later costs money. Structuring now costs a conversation.

First home, honestly.

Five things we tell every buyer in the first meeting.

Some of them are not what you want to hear.

Most people can afford the repayments. They can’t afford the deposit.

So we spend our time on deposit pathways, not on telling you to wait for twenty percent.

Prices rarely wait for you.

Roughly five times your income is where borrowing power starts.

Then debts come off it, and different banks give different answers.

It’s a budget to search with, not a number to offer on.

For a first home, a buyer’s agent is rarely worth the fee.

How a place feels when you walk in matters most, and you can do that part.

We’ll do the data, the digging and the negotiation.

The loan is the easy bit.

Value, offer, contract, settlement. That’s where buyers get hurt, and that’s where we spend our time.

You pick the home. We handle the rest.

Refinancing, honestly.

Five things a broker doesn’t usually say out loud.

We’d rather you heard them before you signed anything.

We won’t move a loan just to move it.

If you already have a good rate and the switch adds nothing structural, we’ll tell you to stay.

Fees and hassle usually eat a marginal gain.

Your current bank can often do what you need.

A top-up, a variation, a reprice. We ask them first.

Moving is the last option, not the first.

Your rate will move. Your discount shouldn’t.

What we negotiate is the margin below the standard rate, and it stays for the life of the loan.

Ask what discount is written into your contract.

The rate on the proposal is where the haggling starts, not ends.

We keep going back to the pricing desk until settlement.

And switching banks is mostly one form: where your pay goes.
